lit.\u0027¿Por qué los aldehídos son más rea: "Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones?"
lit.\u0027¿Qué átomo del grupo carbonilo es: "Which atom of the carbonyl group is electrophilic?"
lit.\u0027\u003c/table\u003e\u003cp class=\":
"

The lower the pKa of HL, the better the leaving group and the faster the acyl substitution.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eDos flechas curvas: e:
"

Two curved arrows: the Nu⁻ pair forms the Nu–C bond and the π pair of the C=O moves onto the oxygen, which becomes an alkoxide (O⁻). The carbon changes from planar sp² to tetrahedral sp³: this is the tetrahedral intermediate. The step is reversible except with strong nucleophiles (H⁻, R⁻).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eDos razones: \u003cb\:
"

Two reasons: electronic (a ketone has two donor alkyl groups that reduce the δ+ on C) and steric (two R groups hinder access; in the sp³ product there is more crowding). Hydration constant: formaldehyde ≈ 2300, ethanal ≈ 1, propanone ≈ 0.0014.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003ecarbo:
"

The C=O carbonyl is planar (sp², 120°) and highly polar: the more electronegative oxygen pulls the π pair (resonance form C⁺–O⁻). The carbon carries a partial δ+ charge and is the site of attack by nucleophiles; the oxygen (δ−) is basic. The π* orbital (LUMO, blue lobes) has its largest coefficient on the carbon.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003ehemia:
"

The (unstable) hemiacetal becomes an acetal with another ROH and acid catalysis (H₂O is lost). Acetals are stable in basic medium: they are used as protecting groups for aldehydes and ketones. In sugars, the cyclic hemiacetal is the pyranose/furanose form.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl alcóxido se proton:
"

The alkoxide is protonated (H₃O⁺ in the acid work-up): the alcohol forms. Depending on the nucleophile the product is a gem-diol (H₂O), a hemiacetal (ROH), a cyanohydrin (CN⁻), or an alcohol by reduction (H⁻) or with a Grignard reagent (R⁻, new C–C bond).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl nucleófilo se apro:
"

The nucleophile approaches the plane of the carbonyl at an angle of about 107° to the C=O bond (Bürgi–Dunitz angle): a compromise between maximum overlap with the π* and minimum repulsion with the O electrons. Bulky R groups block this trajectory (steric hindrance).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn \u003cb\u003eácido:
"

In acids and derivatives (R–CO–L) the tetrahedral intermediate can expel L⁻ and regenerate the C=O: nucleophilic acyl substitution (addition–elimination). Reactivity follows the ability of L as a leaving group (pKa of HL): acyl chloride ≫ anhydride > ester ≈ acid > amide.

"
